speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. Can you describe how this painful ulcer on your leg started and if you have any underlying conditions like diabetes or poor circulation?

speaker: Patient
text: 54-year-old woman. The patient reports a skin lesion on her right leg that has been present for 1 month. The lesion began as a small red spot and has increased in size. She recalls an ant bite at the site before the lesion developed. She has a history of anterior uveitis treated with corticosteroids 8 months ago, as well as Crohn's disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given your history of Crohn's disease, this lesion is highly suggestive of pyoderma gangrenosum, which can be triggered by minor trauma like an insect bite. To confirm this diagnosis and rule out infection, I will request a biopsy of the ulcer edge and a complete blood count. REQUEST TEST: Skin Biopsy

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Skin Biopsy: Histopathology shows neutrophilic infiltration without infection, consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum.

speaker: Doctor
text: The biopsy confirms pyoderma gangrenosum. Do you currently have any active gastrointestinal symptoms, such as diarrhea or abdominal pain, that might indicate a flare of your Crohn's disease?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Painful ulcerative lesion on the right leg. I also have Lesion has a central necrotic base and purplish irregular borders, History of ant bite at the site of the lesion, Pitting pedal edema of the lower extremities, Dilated tortuous veins in both lower legs.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the details. The physical findings of dilated tortuous veins and pitting edema strongly suggest underlying venous insufficiency, which is a common comorbidity in patients with diabetes and hypertension. Given the biopsy has already ruled out infection and confirmed neutrophilic infiltration, I am confident in my assessment. DIAGNOSIS READY: Pyoderma Gangrenosum
